newsitem.title: USA: Fidelity's Pozen known as a trouble-shooter.
newsitem.headline: Fidelity's Pozen known as a trouble-shooter.

text.p: Robert Pozen gained a reputation within Fidelity Investments as a fixer, but he will have his hands full managing the company's vast array of mutual fund managers, analysts said.
As legal counsel, Pozen's face was often seen testifying before U.S. Congressional committees or at the top of his column in Fidelity's quarterly "Focus" magazine sent to retail investors.

Now as head of Fidelity Management & Research Co, the former lawyer will oversee a group of 251 mutual funds with more than $457 billion in assets shaken by the defection of 24 fund managers over the past 18 months.

Fidelity portrayed the management shakeup announced on Monday as merely a change in names moreso than a shift in direction, but analysts were left wondering if Pozen may apply an agenda to the troubled group.
"(Fidelity Chairman) Ned Johnson has always used him in the past to fix all his problems," said David O'Leary, president of Alpha Equity Research.
Pozen gave few clues to his agenda in talks with analysts and reporters on Monday and his background offers few indications in which direction he may take the fund group.
Indeed, Pozen's name was never mentioned in lingering rumors of a new head for the fund group and his appointment caught analysts off guard.

"Somebody like (portfolio manager) George Vanderheiden might be more qualified, but Fidelity may feel they can't spare him from managing $60 billion of funds," said Russel Kinnell, equity fund editor for Morningstar Mutual Funds.
John Bonnanzio, editor of the independent publication Fidelity Insight, said Johnson perhaps made the move to rectify a problem that has festered for too long.

"I would assume that there are things that Ned has agreed that Pozen will do to this group. I would think that there's the recognition that there's some problem there and Pozen has to go in an change the status quo," he said.

One of the most pressing problems is how to stem the exodus of portfolio managers who have left the company. Rumors and reports of the defection of more portfolio managers have persisted over the past few weeks.
Some analysts believe his appointment may simply aggravate the situation.
"I believe Pozen is the wrong choice for that because he does not have an investment background," O'Leary said. "The friction that exists is going to increase significantly."

On the other hand, many analysts said Pozen's predecessor Gary Burkhead, who will now head Fidelity's vast institutional businesses, interferred in portfolio's managers decisions and may have provoked some anger.
"Burkhead did a lot of interfering, as I understand it, and people didn't appreciate that," Bonnanzio said. "Perhaps a kind of lawyer-bureaucrat would be appropriate for this job."

However, analysts expected Pozen to enforce Fidelity's new edict that fund managers stick with an investment style and not try to time the markets - a practice which plagued a number of funds including Magellan last year.
"I assume he'll continue to want a fairly narrow focus, strict discipline from managers," Kinnell said.

Pozen, like his predecessor, will have trouble competiting with hedge funds which can offer more money to Fidelity's talented fund managers, analysts said. Instead, Fidelity should try to offer superior working conditions, they said.

"They have a very, very tough situation on their hands there in respect to competiting with the hedge funds out there," Bonnanzio said. "But not all career decisions are made because of compensation."
((Boston bureau (617) 367-4176))
